content: 1. Enhancing the involvement of front-line staff in rabies surveillance is critical for effective disease monitoring and control. 2. Virus isolation may be necessary to confirm the results of antigen detection tests and to facilitate further amplification or characterization of the isolated virus. 3. Rabies virus can be isolated using cell cultures, such as neuroblastoma cells, or through intracranial inoculation in suckling mice. 4. Whenever possible, virus isolation in animals should be replaced with alternative methods to reduce ethical concerns and improve efficiency. 5. Neuroblastoma cell lines, such as NA C1300, are more susceptible to field isolates of lyssavirus compared to other tested cell lines. 6. Virus isolation in neuroblastoma cell culture is at least as effective as animal inoculation, particularly when dealing with small quantities of the virus. 7. Cell culture isolation significantly reduces the time required for diagnosis, from 10–21 days with the mouse inoculation test to just 2–4 days. 8. However, suboptimal conditions, such as decomposed brain samples, may lead to false-negative results. 9. In the absence of cell culture facilities or molecular methods, animal inoculation remains an option. 10. For rapid results, suckling mice (less than 3 days old) are preferred over weanling or adult mice due to their higher susceptibility to the virus. 11. The observation period can be shortened by inoculating sufficient mice to allow sequential euthanasia and examination of brains using the fluorescent antibody test (FAT), starting 4 days post-inoculation. 12. Molecular methods, such as reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and other amplification techniques, are increasingly important in many countries for rabies diagnosis. 13. If brain tissue is available, FAT or the direct rapid immunohistochemical test (DRIT) should be used for primary diagnosis of viral antigens. 14. Molecular techniques are suitable for confirmatory testing and epidemiological surveys in laboratories with strict quality control and expertise in these methods. 15. Molecular methods can also be used for ante-mortem diagnosis in humans. The use of robust positive or in-process controls is strongly recommended. 16. Ante-mortem diagnosis of rabies in humans can be confirmed using various laboratory methods while the patient is still alive. However, such techniques are strongly discouraged for diagnosing rabies in animals. 17. The sensitivity of diagnostic techniques varies widely depending on the stage of the disease, the patient’s immunological status, intermittent viral excretion, and the training of technical staff. 18. A positive, validated result indicates rabies, but a negative result does not necessarily rule out infection. 19. Viral antigens can be detected using FAT in skin biopsy samples or hair follicles from patients with clinical rabies. 20. Skin samples are typically taken from the nuchal area of the neck, with hair follicles containing peripheral nerves. 21. Examination of multiple sections may be required to detect viral antigens around the base of hair follicles. 22. The quality of the samples is crucial, as the absence of follicles reduces the sensitivity of the test. 23. This technique may not be feasible in all settings due to the need for a cryostat to prepare frozen sections of skin. In such cases, viral RNA detection may be preferable. 24. The FAT of corneal impressions is rarely reliable in most clinical settings and is not recommended as a routine test due to the risk of corneal scarring, especially in patients with encephalitis caused by agents other than rabies. 25. Immunochromatographic methods have been developed to detect rabies virus antigens directly in brain tissue from animals, but these require standardization and stringent quality control before application in human ante-mortem diagnosis. 26. Serological tests are challenging for ante-mortem diagnosis of rabies in humans due to the late appearance of rabies virus-specific antibodies in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). 27. Virus-neutralizing antibodies in the serum of unvaccinated patients or in CSF can be measured using tests such as the rapid fluorescent focus inhibition test (RFFIT) and the fluorescent antibody virus neutralization (FAVN) test. 28. The sensitivity of these assays for ante-mortem diagnosis is low, as virus-neutralizing antibodies typically appear 7–8 days after the onset of clinical symptoms. 29. Viral antibodies are infrequently found in CSF, depending on the clinical stage of the disease. 30. Molecular detection methods are highly sensitive for rabies diagnosis but require standardization and stringent quality control. 31. Serial samples should be tested, as the virus is excreted intermittently. The highest sensitivity is observed with skin biopsies (including hair follicles) and saliva. 32. Virus isolation from saliva or other biological samples is ideal for obtaining a definitive diagnosis and characterizing the virus. 33. The success rate of virus isolation depends on the patient’s immunological status, the intermittent nature of viral excretion, and the number of consecutive passages in cell culture. 34. Specimens may lack infectious virus even during the late stage of the disease. Liquid specimens or swabs should be frozen after collection, and no preservatives should be added to the collection medium. 35. The RFFIT and FAVN tests are recommended for measuring post-vaccination immune responses and determining the need for booster vaccination, as they correlate with protection in animal studies. 36. Virus-neutralization assays are used to evaluate protective antibody levels in immunocompromised patients, assess new vaccines or vaccination schedules, and decide on booster vaccinations based on individual risk factors. 37. ELISAs are useful for routine screening to determine whether an immune response developed after preor post-exposure vaccination, as they are easy to perform. 38. Post-vaccination samples should be tested at or near the time of peak antibody titers, approximately 4 weeks post-vaccination. 39. Serological results from samples collected after this time may be difficult to interpret, as antibody titers can wane rapidly even though animals remain protected against infection. 40. RFFIT and FAVN assays are recommended for international animal movement and trade purposes. 41. ELISAs are suitable for monitoring the antibody response of vaccinated animals within the framework of rabies control. 42. Commercially available ELISA kits should be evaluated under local conditions before use to ensure their performance characteristics meet the requirements of the monitoring program. 43. Participation in quality assurance and proficiency programs is recommended to ensure the validity of results from laboratories performing rabies serology using RFFIT, FAVN, or ELISA.
